steps.body: The data chooses its display: measurements on a number line want a line plot; categories want bars or pictures.
steps.narration: The data chooses its display: measurements on a number line want a line plot; categories want bars or pictures.

widget.prompt: Votes for four trip spots — a category question. Build the fitting display.
widget.successFeedback: Bars fit votes: one per choice, tops on their counts — categories compared at a glance.
widget.partialFeedback: One bar per choice, each top exactly on its vote count.

predict.prompt: Twenty ribbon lengths, measured to the nearest cm. Which display?
predict.reveal: Twenty bars would name every ribbon; the line plot instead shows which LENGTHS repeat — the actual question.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents g2g choose graph.
invariants: A display and its data are the same information in two forms: every measurement appears exactly once, and counts survive the trip into stacks, rows, and bars for g2g choose graph.
misconceptions: Reading a label as a count, dropping repeats while recording, or comparing categories by adding instead of finding the gap.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change to the data would the display be FORCED to show — and what change could it silently hide?

widget.prompt: You measured 20 ribbons to the nearest centimeter and want to see which lengths repeat. Which display fits?

options.label: A line plot over a number line
options.feedback: Correct — measurements live on a number line, and stacked x's make every repeat visible at a glance.

options.label: A picture graph of ribbon drawings
options.feedback: Picture graphs shine for CATEGORIES; centimeter values want their places on a number line.

options.label: A single total of all lengths
options.feedback: One grand total hides every individual length — the repeats you wanted vanish inside it.

options.label: No graph can show repeats
options.feedback: Showing repeats is precisely the line plot's specialty — each repeat adds an x to its stack.

widget.prompt: The class voted for a field-trip spot among four choices. Which display fits the votes?

options.label: A bar graph or picture graph
options.feedback: Correct — votes belong to CATEGORIES, and bars or picture rows compare categories cleanly.

options.label: A line plot over a number line
options.feedback: Trip choices are not numbers on a line — a line plot has nowhere honest to put "the museum".

options.label: A ruler drawing
options.feedback: Rulers measure length; votes need counting per category, not measuring.

options.label: Whichever is prettiest
options.feedback: The DATA chooses the display: categories take bars, measurements take line plots.

widget.prompt: A line plot shows stacks of 2, 4, 3, and 1 x's above 5, 6, 7, and 8 inches. Which measurement is most common?

options.label: 6 inches — its stack is tallest
options.feedback: Correct — "most common" crowns the VALUE under the tallest stack, 4 strong.

options.label: 4 inches
options.feedback: 4 is the tall stack's COUNT of x's, not the measurement those x's record.

options.label: 8 inches — the biggest value
options.feedback: Biggest value and most common value are different crowns; 8's stack holds just 1.

options.label: They are all equally common
options.feedback: The stacks differ in height, and height IS frequency on a line plot.

widget.prompt: Monday has 5 votes and Tuesday has 9 votes. How many more votes on Tuesday?

commonErrors.feedback: That put the days TOGETHER — "how many more" asks for the gap between the bars.
9 is Tuesday's whole count; the question wants only its lead over Monday.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Read the display itself: count what is drawn, and let the stacks, rows, and bars do the remembering.
